Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
Below is a high‑level, step‑by‑step plan for how you could use the two tools you described—**a search tool** that finds relevant API calls on the internet, and **an execution tool** that can run an API call given as a string—to place an order for a burger and fries from McDonald’s.  
The plan is intentionally generic so that it can be adapted to any environment where you have those two capabilities.

---

## 1. Gather Contextual Information

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 1.1 | Ask the user for their **location** (city, ZIP code, or coordinates). | The McDonald’s API will need a location to find nearby restaurants. |
| 1.2 | Ask the user for their **payment method** (card number, PayPal, Apple Pay, etc.). | Payment details are required to complete the transaction. |
| 1.3 | Ask the user for their **delivery address** (if delivery) or confirm they want **pickup**. | Determines whether the order will be delivered or picked up. |
| 1.4 | Ask the user for any **special instructions** (e.g., “no pickles”). | Allows the user to customize the order. |

> **Tip:** Store this information in a temporary data structure (e.g., a dictionary) so you can reference it later when building the API request payload.

---

## 2. Find the McDonald’s Ordering API

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 2.1 | Use the **search tool** to query the web for “McDonald’s online ordering API” or “McDonald’s API documentation”. | You need to locate the official API endpoint(s). |
| 2.2 | Inspect the search results for a **publicly documented API** (e.g., a REST endpoint, GraphQL schema, or SDK). | Public APIs are easier to use; private ones may require authentication keys. |
| 2.3 | If the API is behind a **login** or requires an **API key**, note the authentication flow (OAuth, API key header, etc.). | You’ll need to handle authentication before making calls. |
| 2.4 | Record the **base URL** and any **required headers** (e.g., `Content-Type: application/json`). | These will be used in every request. |

> **Example:**  
> `https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/` (hypothetical base URL)

---

## 3. Authenticate (If Needed)

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 3.1 | If the API requires an **API key**, add it to the headers: `Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>`. | Grants access to the API. |
| 3.2 | If the API uses **OAuth**, perform the OAuth flow to obtain an **access token**. | Required for protected endpoints. |
| 3.3 | Store the **access token** or **API key** for subsequent requests. | Reuse it for all calls. |

> **Note:** If the API is public and does not require authentication, skip this step.

---

## 4. Discover Menu Items

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 4.1 | Use the **search tool** to find the endpoint that lists menu items (e.g., `/menu`, `/products`). | You need to know the IDs of the burger and fries. |
| 4.2 | Execute a **GET** request to that endpoint using the **execution tool**. | Retrieves the menu data. |
| 4.3 | Parse the JSON response to locate the **burger** and **fries** items. | Identify the correct `product_id` or `sku`. |
| 4.4 | Store the **product IDs** and any required **variant IDs** (e.g., size, toppings). | Needed for the order payload. |

> **Example API call string:**  
> ```json
> {
>   "method": "GET",
>   "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu",
>   "headers": {
>     "Authorization": "Bearer <API_KEY>",
>     "Accept": "application/json"
>   }
> }
> ```

---

## 5. Build the Order Payload

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 5.1 | Create a JSON object that includes: | |
| 5.1.1 | `restaurant_id` (from the nearest McDonald’s found in step 2). | Identifies the store. |
| 5.1.2 | `delivery_address` or `pickup_location`. | Determines where the order goes. |
| 5.1.3 | `items`: an array of objects, each containing: | |
| 5.1.3.1 | `product_id` (burger), `quantity`, `variant_id` (size). | |
| 5.1.3.2 | `product_id` (fries), `quantity`, `variant_id` (size). | |
| 5.1.4 | `special_instructions` (if any). | |
| 5.1.5 | `payment_method`: card details or token. | |
| 5.2 | Validate the payload against the API’s schema (if available). | Prevents errors during execution. |

> **Example payload:**
> ```json
> {
>   "restaurant_id": "12345",
>   "delivery_address": "123 Main St, Springfield",
>   "items": [
>     {"product_id": "burger_001", "quantity": 1, "variant_id": "medium"},
>     {"product_id": "fries_001", "quantity": 1, "variant_id": "large"}
>   ],
>   "special_instructions": "No pickles",
>   "payment_method": {
>     "type": "card",
>     "card_number": "4111111111111111",
>     "expiry": "12/25",
>     "cvv": "123"
>   }
> }
> ```

---

## 6. Submit the Order

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 6.1 | Use the **execution tool** to send a **POST** request to the order endpoint (e.g., `/orders`). | Places the order. |
| 6.2 | Include the **payload** from step 5 and the necessary **headers**. | |
| 6.3 | Capture the **response**. | Contains order confirmation, ID, estimated time, etc. |
| 6.4 | Check for **errors** (HTTP status codes, validation errors). | Handle failures gracefully. |

> **Example API call string:**
> ```json
> {
>   "method": "POST",
>   "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders",
>   "headers": {
>     "Authorization": "Bearer <API_KEY>",
>     "Content-Type": "application/json",
>     "Accept": "application/json"
>   },
>   "body": { /* payload from step 5 */ }
> }
> ```

---

## 7. Confirm and Communicate

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 7.1 | Parse the response to extract: | |
| 7.1.1 | `order_id` | Unique identifier for the order. |
| 7.1.2 | `estimated_time` | When the user can expect delivery/pickup. |
| 7.1.3 | `status` | Current state (e.g., “accepted”, “preparing”). |
| 7.2 | Send a **confirmation message** to the user (via chat, email, or SMS). | Keeps the user informed. |
| 7.3 | Offer to **track** the order or **cancel** it if needed. | Enhances user experience. |

---

## 8. Error Handling & Retries

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 8.1 | If the API returns a **4xx** error, display a user‑friendly message and ask for clarification (e.g., wrong address). | Helps the user correct mistakes. |
| 8.2 | If the API returns a **5xx** error, retry the request after a short delay (exponential back‑off). | Handles transient server issues. |
| 8.3 | Log all errors for debugging and analytics. | Improves future reliability. |

---

## 9. Optional Enhancements

| Feature | How to implement | Benefit |
|---------|------------------|---------|
| **Order Tracking** | Poll the `/orders/{order_id}` endpoint periodically. | Keeps the user updated on progress. |
| **Payment Tokenization** | Use a payment gateway (Stripe, Braintree) to tokenize card details before sending to McDonald’s. | Improves security. |
| **Dynamic Menu Updates** | Cache the menu locally and refresh it every X minutes. | Reduces API calls and latency. |
| **Multi‑Restaurant Support** | Allow the user to choose between multiple nearby McDonald’s. | Gives more options. |

---

## 10. Summary Flow Diagram (Textual)

```
User -> Bot
   |
   |---(1) Collect location, payment, address, instructions
   |
   |---(2) Search for McDonald’s API
   |
   |---(3) Authenticate (API key / OAuth)
   |
   |---(4) GET /menu -> Find burger & fries IDs
   |
   |---(5) Build order payload
   |
   |---(6) POST /orders -> Receive order confirmation
   |
   |---(7) Confirm to user (order ID, ETA)
   |
   |---(8) Optional: Poll /orders/{id} for status updates
   |
   |---(9) Handle errors & retries
```

---

### Final Thoughts

- **Security first:** Never expose raw card numbers or sensitive data in logs. Use secure storage and tokenization.
- **Rate limits:** Respect any rate limits imposed by the McDonald’s API to avoid throttling.
- **Testing:** Use sandbox or test environments before going live.
- **Compliance:** Ensure you comply with local regulations (e.g., PCI DSS for payments).

With this plan, you can systematically use the search and execution tools to place an order for a burger and fries from McDonald’s. Happy coding!
